comparator.name: Economics and Business Economics
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted SBE regulations and nominal outline establish the standard Economics pathway. The 180 EC comprises a common 60 EC first year, 60 EC of Economics study and restricted skills choices in year two, then 26 EC abroad, three approved electives, two professional-development skills, thesis preparation and an 8 EC individual thesis. The example uses the nominal order with study abroad in semester five.
components: Economics, Quantitative Economics or Business elective
Writing a Bachelor's Thesis (EBS2080, thesis skills training)

routeSelection.basis: The general programme name does not specify a specialisation. Economics reflects the broad identity through microeconomics, macroeconomics, policy, growth, trade, labour and institutions. The adopted regulations list Economics first. This example follows the standard pathway with study abroad in semester five.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Economics as the defining discipline: microeconomics and macroeconomics in year 1 and Microeconomics: Choices, Markets and Welfare and Macroeconomics and Economic Policy in year 2, used to explain how economies and businesses work
Business-economics foundations common to all students: management of organisations and marketing, accounting and financial reporting, finance, and management and organisational strategy
Quantitative methods, statistics and empirical analysis: Quantitative Methods I to III and the use of mathematics, statistics and data to analyse economic and business questions

The state, public policy and institutions in economics: Public Economics, Macroeconomics and Economic Policy, Economic Growth and Institutions and Institutional Economics, including the role of the state in growth, ageing and public budgets and wage equality
International and global economics: Economics and Global Challenges, International Trade, financial crises and global markets, and the role of international organisations in economics
Sociological and psychological perspectives that the Economics specialisation combines with economics, including consumer behaviour and market outcomes
Independent research and thesis work: Writing a Bachelor's Thesis, the Bachelor's thesis and research projects with staff
adjacent: Emerging Markets specialisation: what drives growth in rising economic powers and other developing economies, how culture and politics shape the business environment, and responsible management and policy decisions in fragile economies, taught through courses on institutions, politics and entrepreneurship, sustainable development, innovation, financing and debates on globalisation

Economics and Management of Information specialisation: information technology, competition and innovation, the economic value of information and the legal, social and ethical questions of IT, taught through courses on the information society, digitalisation and organisations, technology, labour and inequality, knowledge management and systems analysis and design

International Business Economics specialisation: economics and business combined for firms operating across borders, through industrial organisation, financial markets, banking, managerial economics, marketing research, quantitative business, international business and accounting
questions: How do economies and businesses work, and how can economic theory be used to improve businesses and industries and to address global challenges?
How do government policies and economic developments affect consumers and firms, how can governments promote wage equality and how should an ageing population affect public budgets?
How do digital technologies change competition, innovation and the value of information, and what legal, social and ethical questions do they raise?
What drives growth in emerging markets, where do the next business opportunities lie and how can responsible management and policy decisions be made in rapidly changing, sometimes fragile economies?

candidates.label: Emerging markets: economic growth, institutions, politics, culture and responsible management
Economics and management of information: IT, competition, the value of information and legal, social and ethical questions
International business economics: firm strategy, local-to-global conditions and modelling business decisions
candidates.reason: Cross-border strategy, business governance, finance, modelling and digital business are substantial but already supply the organising priorities of the international and digital options. A further business-strategy plan would duplicate those contributions.

candidates.label: Labour inequality and demographic public budgets
candidates.reason: Public Economics, International Macroeconomics and Business & Economy in the Age of AI address redistribution, labour and technology. Their demographic and wage modelling is limited. A separate option would reuse the main economic core without sustained labour or demographic economics.

candidates.label: Economic value of information
candidates.reason: AI decision-making, data management and digital strategy supply related tools, but a sustained information-economics sequence is absent. These courses support the digital option.

candidates.label: Independent economic or business thesis research
candidates.reason: Econometrics and market research support supervised coursework and evidence analysis. Optional independent research supplements these courses. It does not create a distinct 24-course academic direction.

selection.assessment: Three distinct options cover broad economics and business, cross-border institutions and business, and digital tools and organisations. Specialist labour, demographic and information economics remain limits of the comparison. Independent research supplements the plans.

blocks: Economic theory, policy and public economics

Introduction to Economics covers the microeconomics part of the target's Microeconomics (supply and demand, consumer behaviour, the firm, market structure and game theory); its macroeconomics half is a general introduction and is not aligned to another component. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.

Microeconomics & Behavior covers consumer choice, imperfect competition, general equilibrium, market efficiency and externalities, the choices-markets-welfare subject of Microeconomics: Choices, Markets and Welfare; it adds behavioural content the component's title does not mention. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.

International Macroeconomics covers national income, growth, inflation, unemployment and fiscal and monetary policy, the subject of Macroeconomics; its policy and international-trade content is not aligned to a second component. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.

UCR International Macroeconomics includes fiscal/monetary policy and is already paired with the broad first-year macroeconomic component. No second course is assigned to the target’s distinct intermediate stabilisation-policy sequence; this is not absence of all policy content.

Public Economics covers market failure, public goods, taxation, public spending, redistribution and political economy, an important shared subject as the target's Public Economics. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.
UCR covers labour markets in macroeconomics and studies AI’s effects on work. Maastricht provides dedicated labour economics.
Institutions, the global economy and society

The target applies introductory economic tools to inequality, inflation, climate, AI and political challenges. International business and governance provides context; it does not establish the same economic-model foundation.
UCR studies growth in macroeconomics and political institutions separately. Maastricht treats their economic relationship in a dedicated course.
Both study trade theories, policy and integration. UCR also covers foreign investment and business governance, while Maastricht gives trade its own economics course.

Institutional Economics studies transaction costs, property rights, contracts, imperfect information and incentives. Political institutions, business law and general governance do not establish this economic-theory treatment.

QM I explicitly includes functions, optimisation and basic probability/statistics. Mathematical Methods addresses differentiation and related mathematical tools; it does not reproduce the complete economics-specific mathematics/statistics mixture.
Both teach inference, ANOVA and regression. Maastricht combines these with matrix methods and optimisation. UCR covers linear algebra in a separate course in the closest option.

QM III explicitly includes multiple regression, restrictions and sampling/asymptotic reasoning. Econometrics provides that important statistical-method relationship; its estimators and scope differ and it does not cover QM III’s optimisation, integration and dynamic mathematics.
Business, management, finance and business law

Marketing & Consumer Engagement covers marketing strategy, consumer psychology and brand strategy, the marketing half of Management of Organisations and Marketing; its organisation-management half is addressed by the strategy and organisational-behaviour courses, which sit in separate rows. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.

Accounting & Corporate Finance teaches accounting theory and how to read and analyse financial statements, an important shared subject as Accounting and Financial Reporting. Scope, depth, assessment and EC are not identical.
Both study financial markets, risk and asset pricing. UCR also covers banks and financial intermediation.
Information technology, data ethics and law
Academic skills, study abroad and thesis
This unit combines academic writing with philosophy of science, scientific evaluation and open science. General PPD writing or moral philosophy does not establish that combined specific training.

notes.text: UCR offers economics, public policy, finance and quantitative methods, including linear algebra and regression. International Business & Governance includes trade theory and trade policy. Maastricht offers separate specialist courses in trade, labour, growth and institutional economics.

Maastricht requires 26 EC at a partner university and an 8 EC individual thesis with separate preparation. Global Citizenship Skills runs during study abroad and Leadership Skills runs at Maastricht. UCR displays optional independent research alongside the thesis.

The international option studies cross-border business and political institutions. Maastricht’s Emerging Markets specialisation adds regional study and an internship abroad. The digital option develops computing and AI skills, while Maastricht’s information specialisation has dedicated information economics and knowledge-management study.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht Economics and Business Economics combines economic theory with business, finance and quantitative analysis. Students share a first-year foundation and then choose a specialisation. The Economics pathway deepens microeconomics, macroeconomics, public policy, growth, trade, labour and institutions, followed by approved electives, international study and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines economics, business and quantitative methods. The other options add either international institutions and trade or programming and digital strategy. Maastricht’s Economics pathway includes separate specialist economics courses, a period abroad and an individual thesis.
